posts.title: How to Calm a Newborn Baby: Gentle and Effective Soothing Tips for New Moms
posts.content:
Welcoming a newborn is a beautiful experience, but it can also bring questions—especially when your baby is fussy or unsettled. Many new moms often wonder: how can I calm my newborn baby naturally?

The answer lies in creating a soothing, predictable, and comforting environment. In this guide, we’ll share gentle and effective newborn calming techniques that help your baby feel safe, secure, and relaxed.

1. Use Gentle Touch: Hugs, Holding, and Rocking

One of the most effective ways to calm a newborn baby is through gentle touch. Holding your baby close, giving soft hugs, and rocking them slowly can instantly reduce fussiness.

These movements remind your baby of the womb, providing a sense of familiarity and security. Regular physical comfort also strengthens your emotional bond.

2. Play Soft Sounds Like Lullabies or White Noise

Soft, repetitive sounds can work wonders for soothing babies. Lullabies, humming, or white noise help block out sudden disturbances and create a peaceful sleep environment.

White noise, in particular, mimics the constant sounds your baby heard before birth, making it one of the best tools for calming a fussy newborn.

3. Swaddle Your Baby Snugly and Safely

Swaddling is a proven technique to calm newborns. Wrapping your baby snugly in a soft blanket provides warmth and security while preventing the startle reflex that can wake them up.

Always ensure your baby is swaddled safely—snug but not too tight—to allow healthy breathing and hip movement.

4. Maintain Predictable Feeding and Sleep Routines

Consistency is key when it comes to newborn care. Keeping predictable feeding and sleep routines helps your baby feel secure and understand what comes next.

Over time, routines reduce crying, improve sleep patterns, and make daily life easier for both mom and baby.

5. Practice Skin-to-Skin Contact for Bonding and Calm

Skin-to-skin contact is one of the most powerful calming techniques for newborns. Holding your baby against your chest helps regulate their heartbeat, breathing, and body temperature.

It also strengthens the emotional connection between mother and baby, promoting a deep sense of comfort and trust.

6. Create a Calm Space with Dim Lights and Quiet Rooms

Your baby’s environment plays a huge role in their mood and sleep quality. A calm, quiet room with dim lighting helps prevent overstimulation and promotes better rest.

Try to reduce loud noises and bright lights, especially during sleep time, to create a peaceful and soothing atmosphere.

Final Thoughts: Gentle Care Creates a Happy, Calm Baby

Learning how to calm a newborn baby takes time, patience, and love. Every baby is unique, but gentle touch, soothing sounds, consistent routines, and a peaceful environment can make a big difference.

As a new mom, trust yourself—you are your baby’s greatest source of comfort.

Bonus Tip for Moms

If your baby is still fussy, don’t worry. Stay calm, try different soothing techniques, and remember—this phase is temporary. With consistency and care, you’ll discover what works best for your little one.

posts.title: Newborn Sleep Basics Every New Mom Should Know
posts.content:
One of the most common concerns for new moms is newborn sleep. Why does your baby wake so often? How much sleep is normal? Understanding your baby’s sleep patterns can help you feel more confident and less overwhelmed during these early weeks.

Newborn sleep may seem unpredictable, but with the right approach, you can gently guide your baby toward better rest.

1. Understand Newborn Sleep Patterns

Newborns typically sleep 14 to 17 hours a day, but not all at once. Their sleep cycles are shorter, and they wake frequently for feeding and comfort.

This is completely normal and part of their development. Over time, your baby will begin to sleep for longer stretches.

2. Learn Your Baby’s Sleep Cues

Recognizing early sleep cues can make a big difference. Look for signs like yawning, rubbing eyes, fussiness, or staring off into space.

Putting your baby to sleep at the right time helps prevent overtiredness, which can make it harder for them to settle.

3. Create a Simple Bedtime Routine

Even in the early weeks, a simple routine can help signal sleep time. This might include feeding, gentle rocking, dim lights, or a lullaby.

Consistency helps your baby feel secure and understand that it’s time to rest.

4. Make Day and Night Clear

Help your baby learn the difference between day and night. During the day, keep lights on and interact with your baby. At night, keep things calm, quiet, and dim.

This gentle distinction supports the development of a healthy sleep rhythm.

5. Create a Comfortable Sleep Environment

A peaceful sleep space can improve your baby’s rest. Keep the room quiet, slightly cool, and softly lit.

Using white noise or soft sounds can also help block out disturbances and create a soothing atmosphere.

6. Be Patient with the Process

Newborn sleep takes time to develop. There will be good nights and challenging ones, and that’s okay.

With patience, consistency, and love, your baby will gradually learn to sleep better.

Final Thoughts: Rest for Baby and Mom

Understanding newborn sleep basics can make a big difference in your daily routine. While it may feel exhausting at times, remember that this phase is temporary.

Take it one day at a time, and don’t forget to rest when you can—you deserve it too.

posts.title: The Truth About The Fourth Trimester: What No One Tells New Parents
posts.content:
When people talk about pregnancy, they often focus on the three trimesters leading up to birth. There are books, apps, checklists, and countless conversations about preparing for labor and welcoming a baby.

But there is another important stage that receives far less attention: the fourth trimester.

The fourth trimester refers to the first 12 weeks after childbirth. During this time, a newborn is adjusting to life outside the womb, while the mother is recovering from pregnancy and birth. It is a period of major physical, emotional, and lifestyle changes.

Many parents are surprised by how challenging this stage can be. Social media often shows smiling babies and happy family moments, but it rarely shows the sleepless nights, the physical recovery, the emotional ups and downs, and the overwhelming responsibility that can come with caring for a newborn.

If you are currently in the fourth trimester—or preparing for it—you are not alone. Understanding what to expect can make this transition easier and help you approach postpartum recovery with more confidence and compassion.

What Is The Fourth Trimester?

The term fourth trimester describes the first three months after birth.

Although pregnancy officially ends when a baby is born, the body and mind do not instantly return to their pre-pregnancy state. Recovery takes time. At the same time, babies are still developing many of the skills they would have continued practicing in the womb, such as regulating their sleep, feeding patterns, and responses to the world around them.

This period is a major adjustment for both mother and baby.

For Mothers, the Fourth Trimester Often Includes:

  • Physical healing after birth
  • Hormonal changes
  • Sleep deprivation
  • Learning to breastfeed or feed a newborn
  • Emotional adjustments to parenthood
  • Managing household responsibilities while recovering

For Babies, It Involves:

  • Adjusting to light, sound, and touch
  • Learning feeding patterns
  • Developing sleep cycles
  • Building attachment with caregivers

Understanding that this stage is a transition—not a return to normal — can help set realistic expectations.

The Reality Of Postpartum Recovery

One of the biggest misconceptions about childbirth is that recovery happens quickly.

In reality, postpartum recovery is a gradual process that looks different for every mother.

Mothers who have had a cesarean birth may also be recovering from major abdominal surgery, which can require additional time and support.

Healing is not a race. Some women feel physically stronger within a few weeks, while others need several months to recover comfortably.

Sleep Deprivation Is Real

Newborns wake frequently because their stomachs are small and they need regular feeding.

As a result, many parents experience fragmented sleep throughout the day and night.

Lack of sleep can affect:

  • Mood
  • Energy levels
  • Concentration
  • Patience
  • Overall wellbeing

This is why rest is not a luxury during the postpartum period—it is an important part of recovery.

Whenever possible, accepting help from family members or trusted friends can make a significant difference.

The Emotional Side Of The Fourth Trimester

Physical recovery is only one part of the postpartum journey.

Many mothers experience strong emotions after childbirth. These feelings can range from joy and excitement to worry, frustration, sadness, and self-doubt.

Baby Blues

In the first few days after birth, many mothers experience what is commonly called the baby blues.

Symptoms may include:

  • Mood swings
  • Tearfulness
  • Irritability
  • Feeling overwhelmed
  • Anxiety

These feelings are common and are often linked to hormonal shifts, sleep deprivation, and the adjustment to a new routine.

Baby blues typically improve within two weeks.

When To Seek Support

Sometimes emotional difficulties persist or become more severe.

Postpartum depression and postpartum anxiety are real medical conditions that can affect mothers after childbirth.

Signs may include:

  • Persistent sadness
  • Loss of interest in daily activities
  • Intense anxiety
  • Feelings of hopelessness
  • Difficulty bonding with the baby
  • Changes in appetite
  • Trouble sleeping even when the baby is asleep

Seeking professional support is important if these symptoms continue or interfere with daily life.

There is no shame in asking for help. Mental health is just as important as physical health.

Many new parents worry that they are doing something wrong because their baby wants to be held all the time.

In reality, this behavior is completely normal.

Why Newborns Seem To Need Constant Attention

For nine months, babies lived in a warm environment where they were constantly close to their mother. After birth, they are suddenly exposed to new sounds, temperatures, and sensations.

Being held helps babies feel safe and regulated.

During the fourth trimester, many newborns benefit from:

  • Skin-to-skin contact
  • Gentle rocking
  • Swaddling (when done safely)
  • Responsive feeding
  • Close physical comfort

These practices support bonding and can help babies adjust to life outside the womb.

Feeding During The Fourth Trimester

Feeding is often one of the biggest concerns for new parents.

Whether a family chooses breastfeeding, formula feeding, or a combination of both, feeding a newborn requires patience and learning.

Breastfeeding Can Take Time

Breastfeeding is natural, but that does not always mean it comes easily.

Many mothers experience challenges such as:

  • Latch difficulties
  • Sore nipples
  • Concerns about milk supply
  • Cluster feeding
  • Feeding frequently throughout the day

These experiences are common and do not mean a mother is failing.

Guidance from qualified healthcare professionals or lactation consultants can often help address concerns.

Formula Feeding Is Also A Feeding Choice

Some families use formula by choice, while others use it because of medical, personal, or practical reasons.

What matters most is that the baby is fed, growing, and cared for.

Parents deserve support rather than judgment when making feeding decisions.

The Importance Of Building A Support System

One of the greatest myths about motherhood is that mothers should be able to do everything on their own.

The truth is that raising a child has always been a community effort.

Support during the fourth trimester can come from:

  • Partners
  • Family members
  • Friends
  • Healthcare providers
  • Parenting communities

Practical help can include:

  • Preparing meals
  • Assisting with household chores
  • Watching the baby while the mother rests
  • Providing emotional encouragement

Even small acts of support can reduce stress and improve recovery.

Postpartum Self-Care: What Actually Matters

The word self-care is often associated with spa days and luxury treatments.

During the fourth trimester, self-care usually looks much simpler.

It may include:

Prioritizing Rest

Sleep whenever possible and avoid unnecessary pressure to maintain a perfect routine.

Staying Nourished

Regular meals and adequate hydration support recovery and energy levels.

Gentle Movement

Once approved by a healthcare provider, gentle walking and light movement can support physical wellbeing.

Asking For Help

Seeking support is not a sign of weakness. It is a practical part of postpartum recovery.

Being Kind To Yourself

Recovery is rarely linear. Some days will feel easier than others.

Giving yourself grace during this transition is important.

Common Myths About The Fourth Trimester

Myth 1: You Should Bounce Back Quickly

Recovery takes time. Every body heals differently.

Myth 2: Good Mothers Never Feel Overwhelmed

Parenthood can be rewarding and challenging at the same time.

Myth 3: Asking For Help Means You Are Struggling

Support is a normal and healthy part of caring for a newborn.

Myth 4: You Must Enjoy Every Moment

It is possible to deeply love your baby while also finding parts of the postpartum period difficult.

Both experiences can exist at the same time.

A Message To New Parents

The fourth trimester is not simply a recovery period—it is a major life transition.

Your baby is learning how to live in the world, and you are learning how to care for them while also caring for yourself.

There will be moments of joy, uncertainty, exhaustion, and growth. Some days may feel long, but this stage is temporary.

You do not need to have all the answers.

You do not need to be perfect.

And you do not need to go through it alone.

By understanding what the fourth trimester really looks like, parents can replace unrealistic expectations with realistic support, patience, and self-compassion.

Final Thoughts

The truth about the fourth trimester is that it is often messy, emotional, beautiful, exhausting, and transformative—all at the same time.

While much attention is given to pregnancy and birth, the weeks after delivery deserve just as much care and understanding. Postpartum recovery is a journey, not a deadline.

If you are navigating the fourth trimester, remember that healing takes time, support matters, and every small step forward counts.

posts.title: 5 Motherhood Myths Every New Mom Should Stop Feeling Guilty About
posts.content:
Motherhood comes with a lot of advice. Some of it comes from doctors and reliable sources. Some comes from books and parenting experts. And some comes from mothers, grandmothers, friends, neighbours—and the person you barely know who somehow has a very strong opinion about how you should raise your baby.
“You're holding the baby too much.”
“Your baby should be sleeping through the night.”
“Good mothers always know what their baby needs.”
“You must breastfeed, otherwise you're not doing enough.”
“Other babies are already doing this. Why isn't yours?”

With so much advice around us, it can be difficult to know what is actually true. The problem is that some common motherhood beliefs can make mothers feel worried, guilty, or like they are somehow failing. Motherhood is already a huge learning experience. You shouldn't have to carry unnecessary guilt along with it. So let's look at five common motherhood myths—and what the evidence actually tells us.

Myth 1: “A good mother should always know what her baby needs.”

The reality: You learn your baby over time. There is no magical moment when you become a mother and suddenly understand every cry, movement, facial expression, and mood your baby has. You learn. In the beginning, a baby's cry might mean hunger. Or tiredness. Or discomfort. Or simply that they want to be close to you. And sometimes, you won't know. That's normal. Responsive caregiving does not mean understanding every signal perfectly. It means paying attention, trying to understand your child's cues, and responding as best you can. The World Health Organization describes responsive caregiving as noticing, understanding, and responding appropriately to a child's signals. It also emphasizes that healthy development is supported by nurturing interactions between children and their caregivers. That means you don't need to be a perfect mother. You need to be a present and responsive one. You might sometimes misunderstand your baby's cry. You might try feeding when they actually needed sleep. You might change their diaper when they simply wanted a cuddle. That's not failure. That's how you learn your baby. Remember: You don't have to know everything. You just have to keep learning together.

Myth 2: “If you pick up your baby too much, you'll spoil them.”

The reality: Babies need comfort and responsive care. You've probably heard this one before: “Don't pick the baby up every time they cry. They'll get used to being carried.” But a young baby isn't crying to manipulate you. Babies depend on caregivers to meet their needs because they cannot regulate everything on their own. Comforting your baby, holding them, talking to them, and responding to their signals are all part of nurturing care. WHO recommends responsive caregiving during the first three years of life and explains that nurturing interactions support children's health, safety, security, and development. So if your baby wants to be held, it's okay to hold them. If they need reassurance, it's okay to comfort them. If they cry and you respond, you're not “spoiling” them. You're showing them that someone is there when they need help. Of course, as your child grows, they will gradually learn independence too. But independence doesn't have to come from ignoring their need for comfort. Remember: Comfort is not a bad habit. For a baby, comfort is part of feeling safe.

Myth 3: “Every baby should reach milestones at exactly the same time.”

The reality: Development happens at different rates. One baby may start crawling early. Another may take longer. One child may say their first words sooner, while another may take more time. This can make comparisons especially stressful for parents. You might see another baby of the same age doing something your baby isn't doing yet and immediately wonder: “Is something wrong?” Developmental milestones are useful because they help parents and healthcare professionals understand how a child is developing. But they aren't a competition. The CDC explains that developmental milestones are skills that most children achieve by a certain age, while also recognizing that children develop at their own pace. Milestones can provide useful clues about development and help identify when a child may need additional support. So don't use another child as a measuring stick for your own. Instead, pay attention to your baby's overall development and discuss concerns with their healthcare professional when needed. There is an important difference between: “My baby is developing at their own pace.” and “I should ignore a developmental concern.” The first can be completely normal. The second is where professional advice matters. Remember: Milestones are guides—not a race.

Myth 4: “Breastfeeding mothers should never need help.”

The reality: Breastfeeding can be natural and still take practice. Breastfeeding is often described as something that should simply happen naturally. But “natural” doesn't always mean “easy.” A mother may need help with positioning, attachment, feeding frequency, expressing milk, or understanding whether her baby is feeding effectively. WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months when possible, followed by the introduction of complementary foods while breastfeeding continues. But following a recommendation does not mean a mother should be expected to figure everything out alone. If breastfeeding is painful, difficult, stressful, or you're worried that your baby isn't getting enough milk, asking a qualified healthcare professional or breastfeeding counsellor for help is a sensible step. And it's important to remember that mothers can face different circumstances. A mother may breastfeed exclusively. Another may express milk. Another may combine breast milk and formula. Some mothers may not be able to breastfeed. Motherhood shouldn't become a competition over who is doing things “the right way.” The goal is a healthy baby and a supported mother. Remember: Asking for breastfeeding support doesn't mean you're failing. It means you're taking care of yourself and your baby.

Myth 5: “A good mother should be able to do everything herself.”

The reality: Mothers need support too. This might be one of the most damaging motherhood myths. Somehow, mothers are expected to: Feed the baby. Change diapers. Keep the house clean. Prepare meals. Remember appointments. Manage everyone else's needs. Stay patient. Look after themselves. And somehow do all of this without asking for help. But motherhood was never meant to be a one-woman job. The health and wellbeing of a mother matter too. WHO's early childhood development guidance specifically includes support for maternal mental health alongside responsive caregiving and early learning. And struggling emotionally after childbirth is not automatically a sign that a mother is doing something wrong. The ACOG notes that the “baby blues” are common after childbirth and often improve within a few days to one or two weeks. However, more intense or persistent symptoms can be signs of postpartum depression and deserve professional support. So if you need help, ask. If someone offers to hold the baby while you shower, let them. If your family can help with a meal, accept it. If you're feeling overwhelmed, talk to someone you trust. And if you're struggling emotionally for more than the usual early postpartum adjustment—or your feelings are making it difficult to function—reach out to a healthcare professional. Taking care of yourself isn't selfish. It is part of taking care of your family. Remember: You were never meant to carry motherhood alone.

What Motherhood Really Needs

There will always be opinions about how mothers “should” behave. Some advice will be helpful. Some will be outdated. Some will simply be someone's personal experience presented as a universal rule. The important thing is learning to pause and ask: “Is this actually supported by evidence?” And just as importantly: “Is this advice helping me—or simply making me feel guilty?” You don't need to be a perfect mother. You don't need to understand everything immediately. You don't need to compare your baby with every other baby. You don't need to do everything alone. Motherhood is a process of learning, adjusting, asking questions, making mistakes, and trying again. And that's okay. Because your baby doesn't need a perfect mother. They need a mother who cares, responds, learns, and keeps showing up. One day at a time.

A Gentle Reminder for Every Mother

If you've ever felt like you're not doing enough, take a breath. You're learning. If you've ever questioned whether you're doing things “right,” you're not alone. You're learning. If you've ever needed help, you're not weak. You're human. Motherhood isn't about knowing all the answers. It's about having the support to find them. Support. Connect. Nurture. That's what motherhood—and community—should be about.

posts.title: Newborn Sleep: What’s Normal? A Gentle Guide for New Parents
posts.content:
Bringing a newborn home comes with countless beautiful moments—and plenty of questions. One of the biggest is often sleep.

Why does your baby sleep for only a short time before waking up? Why do they seem more awake at night? And should your newborn already be sleeping for longer stretches?

If you have found yourself asking these questions, you are not alone. Newborn sleep can be unpredictable, especially during the first few weeks. You may be tired, unsure whether your baby is getting enough rest, or wondering if you are doing something wrong.

Here is the reassuring truth: newborns are not expected to sleep like adults. Frequent waking, short sleep stretches, and changing patterns are common parts of early infancy.

Let’s explore what newborn sleep usually looks like, why babies wake so often, and how you can support your baby while taking care of yourself, too.

1. How Much Sleep Does a Newborn Need?

Newborns spend much of their time sleeping, but their sleep does not usually follow a predictable schedule.

Some babies sleep for longer stretches, while others wake frequently. According to the UK’s National Health Service (NHS), newborns can sleep for roughly 8 to 18 hours across a 24-hour period, with considerable variation between babies.

Rather than sleeping for one long period at night, newborns often sleep in shorter stretches throughout both day and night.

This happens because they are still developing the patterns that help older children and adults distinguish nighttime from daytime. Their sleep cycles and feeding needs are also different from ours.

What this means for you: Your newborn may sleep for a little while, wake for a feed, settle again, and repeat this pattern several times. That can be normal, even when it feels exhausting.

There is no single sleep schedule that every newborn must follow. Comparing your baby with another baby can create unnecessary worry because each child develops at their own pace.

2. Why Does My Newborn Wake Up So Often?

Frequent waking can be one of the most tiring parts of caring for a newborn. Just when you think your baby has settled, they may wake up again.

There are several reasons this happens.

Their little tummy needs frequent feeding

Newborns have small stomachs and need regular feeds to support their growth. Breastfed and formula-fed babies may have different feeding patterns, but both need appropriate, frequent nourishment during early infancy.

Your baby may wake because they are hungry or ready for another feed. Feeding cues can include moving their head towards the breast or bottle, opening their mouth, bringing their hands to their mouth, or becoming more alert.

Crying can also be a sign of hunger, although it is often a later cue.

They are still adjusting to life outside the womb

Before birth, your baby experienced a very different environment. After birth, they gradually begin adapting to light, sounds, temperature changes, feeding, and new sensations.

Some newborns settle easily, while others need more help to feel comfortable. Gentle holding, rocking, or quiet reassurance may help your baby settle when they need comfort.

They may need a nappy change or a little comfort

Hunger is not the only reason a baby wakes. Your newborn may be uncomfortable, need a nappy change, feel too warm or too cool, or simply want closeness.

Over time, you will begin recognising your baby's individual cues. You do not need to understand every cry immediately. Learning your baby takes time, and it is okay to ask for help.

Remember: Frequent waking does not automatically mean something is wrong or that you have created a bad habit. Newborns need regular care, and their sleep patterns are still developing.

3. Why Is My Baby Awake at Night and Sleepy During the Day?

It can feel frustrating when your newborn sleeps during the day but becomes more alert just as you are ready for bed.

One reason is that newborns have not yet developed a mature body clock, also called a circadian rhythm. This internal system helps the body recognise the difference between day and night.

In the early weeks, your baby may not yet understand when it is time for a longer nighttime sleep.

You can gently help them begin recognising the difference without trying to force a strict routine.

During the day

  • Let natural daylight enter the room.
  • Continue with ordinary household sounds where practical.
  • Offer feeds and interaction when your baby is awake and ready.
  • Allow your baby to sleep when they show signs of tiredness.

During the night

  • Keep lights dim during feeds and nappy changes.
  • Use a calm voice and limit unnecessary stimulation.
  • Keep interactions gentle and quiet.
  • Help your baby settle again after their needs have been met.

These small differences can gradually help your baby become more familiar with day and night. However, this change takes time, and it will not necessarily make your newborn sleep through the night.

There is no need to rush the process. In these early weeks, responding to your baby's needs matters more than following a perfect timetable.

4. What Does Safe Newborn Sleep Look Like?

Understanding your baby's sleep pattern is important, but creating a safe sleep environment is essential every time your baby sleeps.

The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends the following practices to reduce the risk of sleep-related infant deaths.

Always place your baby on their back

Place your baby on their back for every sleep, including naps and nighttime sleep. Side sleeping and stomach sleeping are not recommended for babies.

Choose a firm, flat sleep surface

Use a safety-approved cot, crib, or bassinet with a firm, flat, non-inclined mattress and a fitted sheet.

Avoid using adult beds, sofas, armchairs, inclined sleepers, or soft surfaces as your baby's regular sleep space.

Keep the sleep space clear

Keep pillows, loose blankets, stuffed toys, cot bumpers, and other soft objects out of your baby's sleep area. Although these items may look cosy, they can create risks for a sleeping infant.

Keep your baby close, but in a separate sleep space

Room-sharing is recommended for at least the first six months, with your baby sleeping in their own separate sleep space near you.

This allows you to respond to your baby's needs while maintaining a safer sleeping arrangement.

If your baby falls asleep in a car seat, swing, or stroller, move them to an appropriate, firm, flat sleep surface on their back as soon as it is safe and practical to do so.

A safe sleep space may look simple, but simple is safest.

5. Should I Wake My Newborn for Feeds?

This is a common question, and the answer depends on your baby's age, feeding pattern, growth, and individual health needs.

Some newborns need to be woken for feeds, especially in the early days or if they have not yet regained their birth weight. Babies born prematurely, babies with jaundice, and babies who are not gaining weight as expected may need a specific feeding plan.

Ask your baby's healthcare professional how often your baby should feed and whether you need to wake them.

Once your baby is growing well and feeding is established, your healthcare professional can advise whether it is appropriate to let them sleep for longer stretches.

Do not assume that a long sleep always means your baby is getting enough milk. Feeding effectiveness, weight gain, and wet nappies also help assess whether your baby is receiving enough nourishment.

If your baby is unusually difficult to wake, is feeding poorly, has noticeably fewer wet nappies, or seems unwell, seek medical advice promptly. A newborn with a temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher needs urgent medical assessment.

6. How Can You Cope With Broken Sleep?

Newborn sleep can be demanding for parents, too. Repeated night waking can leave you physically exhausted and emotionally overwhelmed.

You deserve care and rest while caring for your baby.

Here are a few gentle ways to make the early weeks more manageable.

Rest when you can. If possible, take a nap when another trusted adult can care for your baby. You do not have to use every quiet moment to finish household tasks.

Share responsibilities. A partner or family member may be able to help with nappy changes, settling your baby, meals, or household chores. If you are breastfeeding, someone else can still support you in many ways.

Keep expectations realistic. Your home does not need to be perfectly organised, and you do not need to accomplish everything each day. Feeding your baby, recovering, and getting through the day are meaningful achievements.

Ask for help before you feel completely overwhelmed. Speak with someone you trust or your healthcare professional if exhaustion or worry is becoming difficult to manage.

And if you feel frustrated during a difficult night, place your baby safely on their back in their clear cot or bassinet and take a brief moment to calm yourself while ensuring they remain in a safe environment. Never shake a baby.

Looking after yourself is not separate from looking after your baby. Your wellbeing matters, too.

7. When Should You Be Concerned About Your Newborn's Sleep?

Frequent waking and short sleep stretches are common, but changes in your baby's behaviour can sometimes indicate a health concern.

Contact your healthcare professional if you are worried about your baby's feeding, growth, sleepiness, or overall behaviour.

Seek urgent medical attention if your newborn:

  • Is unusually difficult to wake or is not responding as usual.
  • Has trouble breathing or develops blue or grey colouring around the lips or skin.
  • Has a temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher.
  • Is feeding poorly or shows signs of significant dehydration.

Trust your instincts if something does not seem right. You do not need to wait for several symptoms to appear before asking for medical advice.

A Gentle Reminder for Every New Mother

The early days of motherhood can bring love, wonder, uncertainty, and exhaustion—all at once.

Your newborn is learning how to live outside the womb, and you are learning how to understand your baby. Some nights may feel easier than others. Some naps may be short, and some days may feel like one long cycle of feeding, settling, and starting again.

That does not mean you are failing.

You do not need to make your newborn follow a perfect sleep schedule. Focus on responding to their needs, following safe-sleep practices, and seeking professional guidance whenever you are unsure.

With time, your baby's sleep patterns will change. Until then, give yourself the same patience and kindness you give your little one.

At Momkin, we believe motherhood feels lighter when mothers have access to thoughtful products, trustworthy information, and a community that understands their journey.

Because you are learning, too—and you do not have to do it all alone.

Support. Connect. Nurture.

References for further reading

  • NHS: Your baby's sleep patterns
  • NHS: Helping your baby to sleep
  • American Academy of Pediatrics: Safe Sleep

This article provides general educational information and is not a substitute for personalised medical advice from your baby's healthcare professional.
